summary: Defines MIB objects, in SMIv2 format, for managing IEEE 802.5 Token Ring subnetworks with SNMP. It was replaced by RFC 1748.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of gauges for checking on a ring-shaped network where a token is passed around.

questions: how to manage token ring with snmp
subtitle: Management objects for monitoring and controlling IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks using SNMP.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a standard way to monitor and manage IEEE 802.5 Token Ring local area networks using SNMP, with objects that report ring status, errors, and other Token Ring-specific parameters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1743 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with three main tables: the 802.5 Interface Table (status and parameters per interface), the 802.5 Statistics Table (error counters and Ring statistics), and the 802.5 Timer Table (timer values for the protocol). It uses SMIv2 (SNMP Management Framework Version 2) format.
tldr.outcome: This replaced RFC 1231 with an updated version using the newer SMIv2 format. It enables network managers to query and control Token Ring interfaces, detect ring problems, and see detailed error statistics. It was itself replaced by RFC 1748.

today: RFC 1743 was a draft standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1748. The Token Ring MIB has been superseded by updated versions as the SMIv2 framework evolved.

sections.title: Token Ring Network Management
sections.content:
IEEE 802.5 Token Ring is a local area network technology where network devices pass a special token around a logical ring; only the device holding the token can transmit. To manage Token Ring networks, operators need standard ways to monitor ring status, track errors, and control ring behavior via the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

RFC 1743 replaces RFC 1231 with an updated version using SMIv2, the newer structure and syntax for defining managed objects. It defines a set of standard MIB objects that apply to each network interface configured for Token Ring (identified by the interface type iso88025-tokenRing(9)).
sections.plainLanguage: Token Ring is like a circle of computers passing a talking stick around. This RFC describes how to ask them 'is the stick working?' and 'what went wrong?'

sections.title: The Three MIB Tables
sections.content:
The MIB defines three main tables. The 802.5 Interface Table contains state and configuration parameters unique to Token Ring interfaces, including commands to open or close the interface, the ring status bitmask, the ring state (open, closed, opening, closing, or failure), the reason for open success or failure, the negotiated ring speed (1, 4, or 16 Mbps), and the MAC address of the upstream neighbor.

The 802.5 Statistics Table contains 19 different counter objects tracking Token Ring errors and events: line errors, burst errors, AC errors, abort transmission errors, internal errors, lost frames, receive congestions, frame copy errors, token errors, soft errors, hard errors, signal loss, transmitted beacons, ring recoveries, lobe wire faults, removes received, single stations detected, and frequency errors.

The 802.5 Timer Table was already obsolete at publication but is retained for backward compatibility. Each table has one entry per 802.5 interface on the managed system.
sections.plainLanguage: One table says what the ring is doing right now. Another tracks every kind of problem that might happen. A third, no longer used, had timer values.

sections.title: Ring Operations and Error Detection
sections.content:
The interface table includes a dot5Commands object that administrators can write to with values open, reset, or close to control the interface state. The dot5RingStatus bitmask reports ongoing problems: it has values for ring recovery (bit 5), single station (bit 6), remove received (bit 8), auto-removal error (bit 10), lobe wire fault (bit 11), transmit beacon (bit 12), soft error (bit 13), hard error (bit 14), and signal loss (bit 15).

The dot5RingOpenStatus object reports the result of the most recent attempt to insert the interface into the ring, with values for success, bad parameters, lobe failure, signal loss, insertion timeout, ring failure, beaconing, duplicate MAC address, and request failure. The dot5UpStream object reports the MAC address of the upstream neighbor station, essential for troubleshooting ring topology problems.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell a Token Ring interface to join the ring or leave it. The interface reports back what's wrong with the ring or why it can't join.

sections.title: Understanding Ring Error Counters
sections.content:
The statistics table provides detailed error visibility. Line errors indicate corrupted frames detected when the error bit is already set by another station. Burst errors count periods with no signal transitions. Token errors are incremented by the active monitor when it detects an error condition requiring token regeneration.

Soft errors are recoverable by the MAC layer, counted as the number of Report Error MAC frames transmitted. Hard errors count when the interface detects immediately recoverable fatal errors or is transmitting/receiving beacon MAC frames, indicating the ring is recovering from a failure.

Signal loss counts detection of signal loss from the ring. Lobe wire faults detect open or short circuits in the connection path. Remove received counts when the interface received a Remove Ring Station MAC frame request, forcing it to leave the ring. All counters are 32-bit values that wrap around on overflow.
sections.plainLanguage: Each counter tracks a different kind of problem: the ring lost signal, someone's computer can't talk right, the ring had to recover from a crash, or a computer was kicked off.

sections.title: MAC Address Formats and Functional Addresses
sections.content:
Token Ring networks use 48-bit MAC addresses. RFC 1743 specifies that all MAC address representations in the MIB use the canonical order defined in IEEE 802.1a: the address is formatted as if transmitted least significant bit first, even though 802.5 actually transmits most significant bit first. This ensures interoperability with other SNMP MIB modules.

For 16-bit addresses when needed, the upper 4 octets are set to zero. Token Ring also uses functional addresses (group addresses) that multiple stations can recognize; the MIB includes the dot5Functional object, a bitmask of all functional addresses this interface will accept.
sections.plainLanguage: Token Ring uses special addresses. This RFC explains which format to use and how to describe group addresses that multiple computers listen to.
